bal_blocked.text: If one side is blocked, don't force it. Just imagine the breath moving through it.

bal_bp.text: Small trials suggest regular practice may modestly lower blood pressure. Much of that is likely the slow breathing itself.

bal_close.text: That's your practice. Carry the steadiness with you.

bal_hand.text: Right hand up. Fold the index and middle fingers. Your thumb closes the right nostril, your ring finger closes the left.

bal_l_in.text: Thumb on the right. In through the left.

bal_light.text: Fingertips light, just enough to close one side.

bal_release.text: Release the hand. Breathe through both nostrils, and notice how the breath feels now.

bal_rhythm.text: Switching sides slows the breath and gives your attention a steady rhythm to follow.

bal_t_ears.text: With headphones, the breath sound follows the side: left ear, left nostril.

bal_t_pour.text: Let the out-breath spill out slowly, like water poured from a jug.

bal_t_rest.text: If your arm tires, rest the hand for a breath or two. Nothing is lost.

bal_t_track.text: Lost track of the side? Breathe in on the side you just breathed out of.

bal_tradition.text: In yoga tradition, this practice is said to balance body and mind. Notice what balance feels like for you right now.

bal_welcome.text: Welcome to nadi shodhana, alternate nostril breathing. Sit tall, and rest your left hand in your lap.

bandha.text: Gently lift the pelvic floor, and bring the chin slightly down. Hold the breath as if it's resting, not trapped.

bandha_short.text: Root lock. Chin down. Stay soft.

breathe_now_ok.text: Hold only to the first strong urge. If it comes early, tap breathe now. There's nothing to prove.

checkin.text: Let the breath go. Notice how you feel. Warmth, quiet, whatever is here.

close.text: That's your practice. Keep warm, have something hot to drink, and get to bed early. If a fever comes, rest instead, or choose no holds.

cn_close.text: Quiet, low, slow breathing through the nose. Come back to this whenever your nose closes up.

cn_co2.text: As carbon dioxide gently builds, the nose often opens for a while. A small study saw this, much like after exercise.

cn_cycle.text: One side blocked? Congestion naturally swaps sides every few hours. That's your nasal cycle, not the cold getting worse.

cn_gasp.text: If your first breath after a hold is a gasp, the hold was too long. Next time, let go sooner.

cn_how.text: Now the nose-clearing exercise. After a small breath out, pinch your nose, and gently nod your head until you need to breathe.

cn_hum_why.text: Humming vibrates the air in your sinuses. A few hums are plenty; more adds little.

cn_light.text: Now breathe light. Quieter, slightly smaller breaths. Just a touch of air hunger, no more.

cn_light2.text: Keep it small and quiet. A little air hunger is the point, but only a little.

cn_release.text: Release. Breathe in gently through the nose, no big breath. Calm it down within a few breaths.

cn_t_first.text: Notice the first breath after the hold. Gentle, through the nose. No gulp.

cn_t_small.text: Hold after a small breath out, not after a big breath in. It works better, and it is gentler.

cn_temp.text: Relief is often temporary. Come back to this whenever you need it, rather than pushing harder.

cn_welcome.text: Sit tall. Breathe through your nose, or through whichever side is more open. If it's fully blocked, sip a little air through the corner of your mouth.

coh_close.text: That's your practice. Stand up slowly, and take this pace with you.

coh_dizzy.text: If you feel lightheaded, breathe smaller, not faster.

coh_five.text: Studies suggest even five minutes of slow breathing can shift the body toward its calm, vagal state.

coh_light.text: Slow doesn't mean big. Keep each breath light and quiet, as if you could barely hear it.

coh_return.text: Let go of the count. Let the breath find its own rhythm.

coh_sync.text: At around six breaths a minute, your breath and heart rhythm tend to fall into step, and heart-rate variability usually rises.

coh_t_belly.text: Let the belly and lower ribs do the moving. The chest stays quiet.

coh_t_swell.text: Let it feel like a slow swell on the sea. Rising, and falling away.

coh_t_wave.text: Keep it one smooth wave, with no pause at the top or the bottom.

coh_vagal.text: Each long exhale lets the heart slow a little. That's the vagus nerve, your body's brake, doing its work.

coh_welcome.text: Welcome. Find a comfortable seat, and let your breath settle in through the nose.

cool_intro.text: Now cool down. Five slow breaths. In for four, out for eight.

full_science.text: With full lungs, oxygen stays high while carbon dioxide slowly rises. That's where your tolerance is built.

fw_adrenaline.text: In small studies, breathing like this raised adrenaline. Claims about the immune system are still early.

fw_buzz.text: If you feel dizzy, slow down, or stop and breathe normally.

fw_close.text: That's your practice. Notice the warmth, and the clear head. Take it into your day.

fw_r1.text: Round one. Breath of fire. Quick, light breaths through the nose, two or three a second. Belly soft, shoulders still. Keep each breath small.

fw_r2.text: Round two. A few more breaths, and a longer hold.

fw_r3.text: Last round. The longest hold. Stay soft inside it.

fw_rest.text: Breathe easy. Let your heart rate settle before the next round.

fw_t_haaa.text: Can't find the sound? Breathe out a whispered haaa through an open mouth, then close the lips and keep it.

fw_t_hand.text: Next round, try a hand on the lower belly. Only that part should move.

fw_t_snap.text: Each time, snap out, then let go completely. The in-breath takes care of itself.

fw_ujjayi.text: Ujjayi breath: a soft hiss at the back of the throat, like fogging a mirror with your mouth closed.

fw_urge.text: Lock and hold only until the first clear urge. Let the energy settle.

fw_welcome.text: Welcome. This one builds heat. Sit tall, spine long, and breathe through the nose.

g_intro.text: Slow, full breaths through the nose. Then a soft hold, with empty lungs.

hl_close.text: That's the ladder. Breathe easy for a minute before you stand. Two or three times a week is plenty.

hl_contract.text: If your diaphragm starts to twitch, you can end the hold right there. Just tap breathe now.

hl_dive.text: Your heart may slow during the hold. That's the diving reflex, built into every mammal.

hl_how.text: Every hold starts from a comfortable full breath, not a maximal one. The holds stay the same length. The rests get shorter.

hl_last.text: Last hold. Stay soft right to the end.

hl_rests.text: In the rests, breathe slow and easy. No big breaths, no fast breathing.

hl_rule.text: If a hold ever starts to feel like a maximum effort, end the table there. Training happens below your limit.

hl_soft.text: Soften the face. Shoulders down. Holding the breath is a relaxation skill.

hl_spleen.text: Over a few holds, the spleen squeezes out a small reserve of red blood cells. A real effect, but a small one.

hl_t_scan.text: In the next hold, scan the jaw, the shoulders, the hands and the hips. Let each one go.

hl_t_small.text: Normal-size breaths in the rests. Nothing big, nothing fast.

hl_welcome.text: Welcome to the hold ladder, a dry breath-hold table from freediving. Sit or lie down. Never in water.

hl_why.text: The same hold with less rest each time lets carbon dioxide build a little more. That's what you're getting used to.

hum_again.text: Three last hums. Long and low.

hum_intro.text: Humming breath. Breathe in through the nose, then hum the whole exhale, lips closed, jaw soft. Let the sound fill your head.

ladder_intro.text: Now we lengthen the breath, one step at a time. Four counts in, four counts out. Follow the circle.

ladder_up2.text: Six in, six out. Smooth and even.

n_and_pause_up_to_fifteen_seconds_throat.text: And pause, up to fifteen seconds. Throat soft.

n_and_pause_up_to_fifty_seconds_throat_s.text: And pause, up to fifty seconds. Throat soft.

n_and_pause_up_to_forty_seconds_throat_s.text: And pause, up to forty seconds. Throat soft.

n_and_pause_up_to_one_minute_throat_soft.text: And pause, up to one minute. Throat soft.

n_and_pause_up_to_thirty_seconds_throat_.text: And pause, up to thirty seconds. Throat soft.

n_back_to_four_in_six_out.text: Back to four in, six out.

n_breathe_in_all_the_way_to_the_top_and_.text: Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. Fifteen seconds.
Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. Forty-five seconds.
Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. Forty seconds.
Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. One minute.
Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. Ten seconds.
Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. Thirty seconds.
Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. Twenty-five seconds.
Breathe in, all the way to the top, and hold. Twenty seconds.

n_breathe_in_comfortably_full_not_to_the.text: Breathe in, comfortably full. Not to the top.

n_breathe_rest_a_minute_and_a_half.text: Breathe. Rest, a minute and a half.

n_breathe_that_was_the_last_one.text: Breathe. That was the last one.

n_five_hums_in_for_four_then_hum_it_all_.text: Five hums. In for four, then hum it all out.

n_five_minutes_in_top_up_and_a_long_slow.text: Five minutes. In, top up, and a long, slow breath out.

n_five_pauses_growing_from_thirty_second.text: Five pauses, growing from thirty seconds to a minute.

n_five_pauses_of_up_to_fifteen_seconds.text: Five pauses of up to fifteen seconds.

n_four_in_five_out_ten_breaths.text: Four in, five out. Ten breaths.

n_four_in_four_out_twelve_rounds_we_star.text: Four in, four out. Twelve rounds. We start on the left.

n_four_rounds_in_through_the_nose_for_fo.text: Four rounds. In through the nose for four, hold for seven, and whoosh out through the mouth for eight.

n_half_a_minute_of_calm_breathing_then_t.text: Half a minute of calm breathing. Then the first hold.

n_hold_five_of_six_forty_five_seconds.text: Hold five of six. Forty-five seconds.

n_hold_five_of_six_one_minute.text: Hold five of six. One minute.

n_hold_five_of_six_twenty_five_seconds.text: Hold five of six. Twenty-five seconds.

n_hold_four_of_six_forty_five_seconds.text: Hold four of six. Forty-five seconds.

n_hold_four_of_six_one_minute.text: Hold four of six. One minute.

n_hold_four_of_six_twenty_five_seconds.text: Hold four of six. Twenty-five seconds.

n_hold_lungs_empty_for_up_to_forty_five_.text: Hold, lungs empty, for up to forty-five seconds.

n_hold_lungs_empty_for_up_to_one_minute.text: Hold, lungs empty, for up to one minute.

n_hold_lungs_empty_for_up_to_one_minute_.text: Hold, lungs empty, for up to one minute fifteen.
Hold, lungs empty, for up to one minute forty.
Hold, lungs empty, for up to one minute twenty.

n_hold_lungs_empty_for_up_to_thirty_five.text: Hold, lungs empty, for up to thirty-five seconds.

n_hold_lungs_empty_for_up_to_twenty_five.text: Hold, lungs empty, for up to twenty-five seconds.

n_hold_one_of_six_forty_five_seconds.text: Hold one of six. Forty-five seconds.

n_hold_one_of_six_one_minute.text: Hold one of six. One minute.

n_hold_one_of_six_twenty_five_seconds.text: Hold one of six. Twenty-five seconds.

n_hold_six_of_six_forty_five_seconds.text: Hold six of six. Forty-five seconds.

n_hold_six_of_six_one_minute.text: Hold six of six. One minute.

n_hold_six_of_six_twenty_five_seconds.text: Hold six of six. Twenty-five seconds.

n_hold_three_of_six_forty_five_seconds.text: Hold three of six. Forty-five seconds.

n_hold_three_of_six_one_minute.text: Hold three of six. One minute.

n_hold_three_of_six_twenty_five_seconds.text: Hold three of six. Twenty-five seconds.

n_hold_two_of_six_forty_five_seconds.text: Hold two of six. Forty-five seconds.

n_hold_two_of_six_one_minute.text: Hold two of six. One minute.

n_hold_two_of_six_twenty_five_seconds.text: Hold two of six. Twenty-five seconds.

n_in_for_four_out_for_six_six_breaths.text: In for four, out for six. Six breaths.

n_in_for_four_out_for_six_small_and_quie.text: In for four, out for six, small and quiet. About six minutes.

n_instead_of_pausing_lengthen_the_out_br.text: Instead of pausing, lengthen the out-breath. In for four, out for eight.

n_now_four_in_eight_out_ten_rounds.text: Now four in, eight out. Ten rounds.

n_now_four_in_six_out_we_ll_stay_here_fo.text: Now four in, six out. We'll stay here for about six minutes.

n_now_out_for_eight_eight_breaths.text: Now out for eight. Eight breaths.

n_pinch_and_nod_let_go_at_the_first_clea.text: Pinch, and nod. Let go at the first clear urge.

n_round_one_five_slow_breaths_then_rest.text: Round one. Five slow breaths, then rest.

n_round_one_small_breath_in_small_breath.text: Round one. Small breath in, small breath out.

n_round_three_five_slow_breaths_then_res.text: Round three. Five slow breaths, then rest.

n_round_two_five_slow_breaths_then_rest.text: Round two. Five slow breaths, then rest.

n_round_two_small_breath_in_small_breath.text: Round two. Small breath in, small breath out. Pinch and nod, until moderate air hunger.

n_six_slow_breaths_in_for_four_out_for_s.text: Six slow breaths. In for four, out for six.

n_slowly_let_your_head_tip_toward_the_ri.text: Slowly let your head tip toward the right shoulder.

n478_drift.text: Let go of counting. Let the breath be as slow and as small as it wants.

n478_end.text: Nothing more to do. Stay here as long as you like.

n478_exhale.text: Your heart slows a little on every exhale. A longer exhale gives it more time to settle.

n478_mind.text: Counting gives a busy mind something simple to hold on to.

n478_ratio.text: If the hold feels long, let it go early. The ratio matters more than the seconds.

n478_t_clouds.text: If thoughts come, let them drift past. No need to follow them.

n478_t_heavy.text: Let your body get a little heavier with every out-breath, sinking into the bed.

n478_tongue.text: Next, four, seven, eight. Rest the tip of your tongue behind your upper front teeth, and keep it there.

n478_welcome.text: Welcome. Lie down if you can, and let the bed take your weight. This is a wind-down, not a test.

nh_notice.text: No hold this time. Breathe easily, and notice how you feel.

nose_short.text: Breathe only through your nose, slow and quiet.

nt_a_light_stomach_it_also_makes_a_good_.text: A light stomach. It also makes a good wind-down before sleep.

nt_a_little_air_hunger_is_fine_warm_hand.text: A little air hunger is fine. Warm hands, yawning and a slower pulse are common.

nt_a_racing_heart_jerky_breathing_or_bre.text: A racing heart, jerky breathing, or breathing bigger afterwards means the hold was too long.

nt_a_rolled_jumper_behind_your_lower_bac.text: A rolled jumper behind your lower back, feet flat, and the headrest not pushing your chin down.

nt_a_throbbing_headache_or_migraine_aura.text: A throbbing headache or migraine aura, during descent, pregnancy, heart or lung disease, or anaemia: choose No pauses.

nt_a_warm_buzz_in_the_face_while_humming.text: A warm buzz in the face while humming is normal.

nt_add_about_five_seconds_a_week_and_onl.text: Add about five seconds a week, and only if the last round still felt comfortable.

nt_after_a_month_up_to_eight_rounds_of_4.text: After a month, up to eight rounds of 4, 7, 8.

nt_arm_getting_tired_rest_the_hand_for_a.text: Arm getting tired? Rest the hand for a breath or two. Nothing is lost.

nt_bearing_down_with_the_throat_a_soft_t.text: Bearing down with the throat? A soft throat. Nothing pushes.

nt_big_forced_in_breaths_breathe_in_with.text: Big, forced in-breaths? Breathe in with no more effort than at rest.

nt_big_or_fast_breaths_in_the_rests_norm.text: Big or fast breaths in the rests? Normal-size breaths with a long out-breath.

nt_breathe_in_through_the_nose_if_it_hel.text: Breathe in through the nose. If it helps, let the out-breath leave through barely parted lips.

nt_breathe_through_the_more_open_side_or.text: Breathe through the more open side, or sip through the corner of your mouth if fully blocked.

nt_breathing_big_because_the_pace_is_slo.text: Breathing big because the pace is slow? Slower, not bigger. Small, quiet breaths.

nt_breathing_big_to_get_more_air_slower_.text: Breathing big to get more air? Slower, not bigger.

nt_breathing_in_through_the_mouth_in_thr.text: Breathing in through the mouth? In through the nose, quietly. The whoosh is only on the way out.

nt_brief_lightheadedness_early_on_is_com.text: Brief lightheadedness early on is common.

nt_can_t_find_ujjayi_breathe_out_a_whisp.text: Can't find ujjayi? Breathe out a whispered haaa through an open mouth, as if fogging a mirror, then close the lips and keep the sound.

nt_chest_and_shoulders_heaving_only_the_.text: Chest and shoulders heaving? Only the lower belly moves.

nt_chest_and_shoulders_lifting_let_the_b.text: Chest and shoulders lifting? Let the belly and lower ribs move; the chest stays quiet.

nt_chin_poking_forward_let_the_back_of_t.text: Chin poking forward? Let the back of the neck lengthen.

nt_diaphragm_contractions_late_in_a_hold.text: Diaphragm contractions late in a hold are common. They are a fine moment to end it.

nt_dizziness_nausea_or_anxiety_stop_brea.text: Dizziness, nausea or anxiety: stop, breathe normally, and choose Gentle next time.

nt_doing_lots_of_rounds_four_at_a_time_f.text: Doing lots of rounds? Four at a time for the first month, then up to eight.

nt_dry_only_seated_or_lying_never_in_or_.text: Dry only: seated or lying, never in or near water, never while driving.

nt_fever_chest_symptoms_breathlessness_p.text: Fever, chest symptoms, breathlessness, pregnancy, high blood pressure, or feeling faint: choose No holds.

nt_fever_chest_symptoms_pregnancy_epilep.text: Fever, chest symptoms, pregnancy, epilepsy, heart disease or high blood pressure: choose No holds, or a calm practice.

nt_for_4_7_8_the_tongue_tip_rests_behind.text: For 4, 7, 8, the tongue tip rests behind the upper front teeth the whole time.

nt_forcing_a_blocked_side_don_t_imagine_.text: Forcing a blocked side? Don't. Imagine the breath moving through it.

nt_gasping_afterwards_first_breath_gentl.text: Gasping afterwards? First breath gentle, through the nose. A gasp means the hold was too long.

nt_gasping_on_the_first_breath_the_hold_.text: Gasping on the first breath? The hold was too long: shorten the next one, or end the table.

nt_going_too_fast_rhythm_before_speed_sl.text: Going too fast? Rhythm before speed. Slower is fine.

nt_gulping_the_in_breaths_fill_the_belly.text: Gulping the in-breaths? Fill the belly through the nose, then a small top-up sip, shoulders heavy.

nt_headphones_in_nothing_here_is_audible.text: Headphones in. Nothing here is audible to the people next to you.

nt_heart_or_lung_disease_high_blood_pres.text: Heart or lung disease, high blood pressure, pregnancy, panic disorder, or when you are unwell.

nt_holding_after_a_big_breath_in_hold_af.text: Holding after a big breath in? Hold after a small breath out.

nt_holding_hard_through_the_seven_let_go.text: Holding hard through the seven? Let go early. The ratio matters more than the seconds.

nt_humming_loud_with_a_tight_jaw_a_low_q.text: Humming loud with a tight jaw? A low, quiet hum; molars apart, lips touching lightly.

nt_if_counting_keeps_you_alert_drop_it_a.text: If counting keeps you alert, drop it and keep only the long out-breaths.

nt_if_focusing_on_the_breath_makes_you_a.text: If focusing on the breath makes you anxious, keep your eyes open and anchor on sounds instead, or stop.

nt_if_it_feels_like_too_much_air_try_res.text: If it feels like too much air, try Resonance instead.

nt_if_the_throb_gets_worse_in_the_pauses.text: If the throb gets worse in the pauses, skip them.

nt_in_bed_lights_low_press_begin_then_pu.text: In bed, lights low. Press Begin, then put the phone face down.

nt_in_through_the_nose_out_through_the_m.text: In through the nose, out through the mouth.

nt_kapalabhati_from_the_chest_snap_the_l.text: Kapalabhati from the chest? Snap the lower belly in; let the in-breath happen.

nt_keep_one_to_three_sighs_as_a_pocket_r.text: Keep one to three sighs as a pocket reset for tense moments.

nt_keep_the_holds_comfortable_deeper_is_.text: Keep the holds comfortable. Deeper is for people who already practise breath holds.

nt_locks_a_gentle_lift_of_the_pelvic_flo.text: Locks: a gentle lift of the pelvic floor, not a squeeze; let the chin lower rather than pressing it down. Release both before the next breath.

nt_losing_track_of_the_sides_breathe_in_.text: Losing track of the sides? Breathe in on the side you just breathed out of.

nt_many_people_feel_calmer_after_one_to_.text: Many people feel calmer after one to three sighs.

nt_mornings_on_an_empty_stomach_two_to_t.text: Mornings, on an empty stomach: two to three hours after eating.

nt_nose_blocked_try_clear_nose_first_458.text: Nose blocked? Try Clear Nose first.

nt_once_a_day_at_most_two_or_three_times.text: Once a day at most; two or three times a week is plenty.

nt_one_side_often_flows_more_easily_that.text: One side often flows more easily. That is the normal nasal cycle.

nt_over_weeks_lengthen_the_out_breath_fu.text: Over weeks, lengthen the out-breath further. Holds come later, and not with high blood pressure or heart disease.

nt_over_weeks_more_breaths_per_round_bef.text: Over weeks, more breaths per round before longer holds.

nt_panic_disorder_pregnancy_or_heart_dis.text: Panic disorder, pregnancy or heart disease: shorten the hold, or skip 4, 7, 8 and keep the long out-breaths.

nt_pausing_at_the_top_or_bottom_keep_it_.text: Pausing at the top or bottom? Keep it one smooth, continuous wave.

nt_pick_the_level_whose_hold_is_about_ha.text: Pick the level whose hold is about half your relaxed, not all-out, maximum.

nt_practised_regularly_relaxation_may_re.text: Practised regularly, relaxation may reduce how often headaches come. Try it at home on headache-free days too.

nt_pregnancy_epilepsy_high_blood_pressur.text: Pregnancy, epilepsy, high blood pressure or heart disease, hernia, recent surgery, glaucoma, or a fever. Evenings, if it keeps you awake.

nt_pressing_too_hard_a_feather_light_tou.text: Pressing too hard? A feather-light touch on the soft side of the nostril.

nt_pulling_the_in_breath_in_snap_out_the.text: Pulling the in-breath in? Snap out, then let go. The in-breath happens by itself.

nt_pushing_to_strong_air_hunger_with_a_c.text: Pushing to strong air hunger? With a cold, moderate is the limit.

nt_re_check_your_relaxed_maximum_every_w.text: Re-check your relaxed maximum every week or two.

nt_repeat_whenever_you_need_it_rather_th.text: Repeat whenever you need it, rather than holding longer.

nt_rushing_the_out_breath_an_audible_unh.text: Rushing the out-breath? An audible, unhurried sigh, about twice as long as the in-breaths.

nt_seated_or_lying_five_minutes_ideally_.text: Seated or lying. Five minutes, ideally daily: that was the dose in the study.

nt_seated_or_lying_kapalabhati_goes_best.text: Seated or lying. Kapalabhati goes best on an empty stomach.

nt_seated_with_your_back_supported_or_ly.text: Seated with your back supported, or lying down. Any time of day.

nt_short_and_daily_beats_long_and_occasi.text: Short and daily beats long and occasional. Many people build from five minutes to fifteen or twenty.

nt_sit_tall_if_your_arm_tires_prop_the_r.text: Sit tall. If your arm tires, prop the right elbow on your left hand or a cushion.

nt_sit_upright_never_standing_a_hand_on_.text: Sit upright, never standing. A hand on the lower belly helps at first.

nt_sit_upright_not_straight_after_a_meal.text: Sit upright, not straight after a meal.

nt_skip_it_or_go_gentle_if_1qua4zg.text: Skip it, or go gentle, if…

nt_some_relief_or_simply_feeling_calmer_.text: Some relief, or simply feeling calmer, is a good result.

nt_speeding_up_slow_down_fast_sighing_tu.text: Speeding up? Slow down. Fast sighing turns into over-breathing.

nt_squeezing_the_throat_in_ujjayi_whispe.text: Squeezing the throat in ujjayi? Whisper-level: you hear it, your neighbour doesn't.

nt_stop_if_you_feel_breathless_lighthead.text: Stop if you feel breathless, lightheaded or tight in the chest.

nt_stop_if_you_feel_lightheaded_or_get_h.text: Stop if you feel lightheaded, or get head pressure, chest pain or changes in your vision.

nt_straining_in_the_holds_hold_as_if_the.text: Straining in the holds? Hold as if the breath is resting. Soft throat.

nt_straining_in_the_pauses_pause_rather_.text: Straining in the pauses? Pause, rather than hold: soft throat, nothing pushing.

nt_teacher_s_notes_for_turn_the_tide_z3j.text: Teacher's notes for Turn the Tide.

nt_tensing_up_as_the_hold_goes_on_scan_t.text: Tensing up as the hold goes on? Scan the jaw, shoulders, hands and hips. Let each one go.

nt_the_holds_are_optional_switch_to_no_h.text: The holds are optional: switch to No holds once you are properly ill, not just getting there.

nt_the_nose_often_opens_for_a_few_minute.text: The nose often opens for a few minutes, then closes again. That is expected.

nt_tingling_and_lightness_after_kapalabh.text: Tingling and lightness after kapalabhati are common. Dizziness means stop and breathe.

nt_tingling_dizziness_a_light_headache_o.text: Tingling, dizziness, a light headache or tight hands mean the breaths are too big: make them smaller.

nt_tingling_or_lightness_slow_the_out_br.text: Tingling or lightness: slow the out-breath down.

nt_warmth_tingling_and_a_raised_heart_ra.text: Warmth, tingling and a raised heart rate that settles within a minute are common.

nt_water_within_reach_on_long_journeys_s.text: Water within reach. On long journeys, stand up and walk every 30 to 60 minutes.

nt_when_4_in_6_out_feels_easy_simply_pra.text: When 4 in, 6 out feels easy, simply practise for longer. A longer session matters more than a slower count.

nt_with_a_cold_or_a_blocked_nose_resonan.text: With a cold or a blocked nose. Resonance gives most of the same calm.

r1_intro.text: Round one. Kapalabhati. Short, sharp exhales through the nose, pulled from the belly. The inhale takes care of itself. Keep your face soft.

r1_permission.text: If you feel dizzy, or the urge to breathe gets strong, breathe normally. You can end any round, any time.

r2_hunger.text: Soften your jaw, your eyes, your hands. When you want to breathe, breathe.

r2_intro.text: Round two. A few more breaths this time, and a longer hold. Many people find the second hold easier than the first.

r3_after.text: Three rounds done. Notice the warmth in your hands and face, and the quiet behind it.

r3_intro.text: Last round. Let this be the easiest one.

r3_still.text: Nothing to do. Just the stillness of an empty breath.

release.text: And let it go. Breathe naturally.

ribs.text: Let the ribs widen to the sides, like a band stretching. Shoulders still, belly soft. Breathe in with no more effort than at rest.

sigh_close.text: Let your breath return to normal. One or two sighs, any time today, can be a small reminder of this.

sigh_heart.text: Your heart slows a little on every exhale. Making the exhale long leans the whole system toward calm.

sigh_how.text: Breathe in through the nose. At the top, take a second, smaller sip to fill the lungs completely. Then let it all go through the mouth, slowly.

sigh_science.text: In a month-long Stanford study, five minutes of daily cyclic sighing lifted mood more than mindfulness meditation.

sigh_soft.text: If you feel tingly, slow the exhale down. Calm, not forced.

sigh_t_audible.text: An audible sigh is welcome. Let the sound leave with the air.

sigh_t_shoulders.text: Shoulders heavy as you breathe in. Only the lungs fill.

sigh_t_twice.text: Let the out-breath last about twice as long as the in-breaths.

sigh_welcome.text: Welcome. This is the cyclic sigh: a double breath in, and a long, slow breath out.

story_co2.text: A moment on what just happened. Fast breathing adds very little oxygen; your blood is already almost full. What it does is blow off carbon dioxide. With less of it, your blood turns slightly alkaline, the vessels in your head narrow a little, and you may feel tingling or lightness. That's why the hold felt easy at first. The urge to breathe comes mostly from carbon dioxide rising, not from oxygen falling. It's also why this practice belongs on dry land, seated or lying down: the warning signal arrives late.

story_hum.text: Here's why we hum. Nitric oxide collects in your sinuses, but it barely moves while you breathe quietly. Humming makes the air in them vibrate, and that flushes it out. In one study, humming raised the nitric oxide in the nose about fifteen-fold, compared with a quiet exhale. The boost is biggest on the first hums, and the sinuses take a few minutes to fill again, so we'll hum once more at the end. In cell studies, nitric oxide slows the virus behind most colds. No trial has shown that humming prevents one. But it's a pleasant way to look after your nose.

story_kox.text: Here's a study that changed how scientists think about breathing. In 2014, a group of young men in the Netherlands trained for ten days in a method like this one: fast breathing with long holds, cold exposure and meditation. Then they, and an untrained group, were injected with a purified bacterial toxin that briefly causes flu-like symptoms. The trained group released a surge of adrenaline. Their inflammatory signals were lower, their anti-inflammatory signals higher, and they felt less unwell. It was a small study, in healthy volunteers, with a toxin rather than a virus. Not a cure for a cold. But a sign that your breath can talk to your immune system.

story_nose.text: While you settle, a word about the nose. It warms and moistens every breath, and its fine hairs and mucus catch dust and germs before they reach your lungs. Your sinuses also release a gas called nitric oxide, and it travels down with every breath you take through the nose. In the lab, nitric oxide helps the airways defend themselves. Breathe through your mouth, and you skip all of that. So for the next few minutes, nose only.

story_vagus.text: As you breathe out slowly, your heart slows a little. On every inhale it speeds up; on every exhale it eases off. That rhythm is steered by the vagus nerve, your body's brake pedal, and long exhales give it more to do. Why does that matter today? In a classic study, people under more stress were more likely to catch a cold when they were exposed to the virus. And people who slept less than six hours were about four times more likely to get sick than those who slept seven or more. Calm and sleep are the real medicine here.

t_anchor.text: Notice where the breath is easiest to feel. Cool air in at the nostrils, slightly warmer air out.

t_belly_only.text: Face and shoulders still. Only the belly moves.

t_eyes.text: Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest softly on the floor.

t_first_breath.text: Keep that first breath calm. If it came as a gasp, make the next hold shorter.

t_hold_guide.text: Let go whenever you need to. The timer is a guide, not a test.

t_notice.text: Notice what's different, without needing anything to be different.

t_slower_fine.text: Slower is fine. Rhythm matters more than speed.

t_wander.text: If your mind has wandered, that's what minds do. Noticing is the practice. Come back to the next breath.

tide_t_easy_in.text: Between rounds, breathe in with no more effort than at rest.

tide_t_hum.text: A low, quiet hum. Molars apart, lips touching lightly. Feel it buzz in your face.

welcome.text: Welcome. Sit tall, or lie down. Let your eyes close, and let the day go quiet for a few minutes.

ws_brow.text: Unknit the brow. Soften around the eyes, and across the scalp.

ws_checkin.text: Notice your head, your jaw, your shoulders. Whatever has eased, let it stay eased.

ws_close.text: That's your practice. Sip some water, and keep taking your usual medication as you normally would. Come back to this whenever you need it.

ws_face_why.text: Jaw, brow and shoulders often tighten around a headache. Letting them soften may ease some of the pressure.

ws_h_brow.text: Smooth the brow. Soften behind the eyes.

ws_h_hands.text: Let your hands grow heavy in your lap.

ws_h_jaw.text: Let the jaw hang soft. Teeth apart.

ws_h_last.text: Last pause. Nothing to prove. Let go whenever you like.

ws_h_sway.text: If you're on a train, feel its sway. Let the movement rock you, rather than holding against it.

ws_jaw.text: Lips together, teeth apart. Let the tongue rest on the floor of the mouth.

ws_long_why.text: A longer out-breath gives the heart more time to slow, and the body more time to settle.

ws_neck.text: Let the back of the neck lengthen, the chin tipping very slightly down.

ws_pain.text: In lab studies, slow breathing with a longer out-breath dulled pain a little. It may take the edge off.

ws_pause_intro.text: Now a few soft pauses. Breathe in to about two-thirds full, then simply pause. Throat relaxed, nothing pushing. Let the jaw and shoulders go.

ws_shoulders.text: On each breath out, let the shoulders drop a little further.

ws_silent.text: Everything here is silent. Nose only, small breaths. No one around you needs to know you're doing this.

ws_skip.text: If the throbbing grows, or your head feels fuller, skip the pauses and just lengthen the out-breath.

ws_small.text: Slower, not bigger. Over-breathing can make you light-headed.

ws_stress.text: Stress itself raises inflammatory signals. Whether breathing reaches the immune system directly is still uncertain. Regular practice is where any benefit lies.

ws_t_shoulders.text: Check the shoulders again. They've probably crept up. Let them drop.

ws_t_sounds.text: Let the sounds around you, the engine, the voices, the rails, become part of the background. Nothing to fix.

ws_t_window.text: If your eyes are open, let them rest on the window. Let the view pass by, without following it.

ws_vagal.text: A long out-breath shifts the heart toward its calmer, vagal rhythm. The same nerve, stimulated electrically, can dampen inflammation.

ws_welcome.text: Welcome. Sit back, head against the headrest if you can, feet flat on the floor. Eyes down, or closed. If you have water, take a sip now.
